```{python}
#| label: setup
# Every number in this paper is computed here and inserted by reference. None is
# typed into the prose. That makes "regenerate the paper" and "check the paper"
# the same operation, which is the only version of reproducibility that survives
# a revision.
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import duckdb
import pandas as pd

from softverse.stata.builtins import curated

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent if "__file__" in dir() else "."))
from exhibits import figure, table  # noqa: E402

TALLY = Path("../build/tally")
con = duckdb.connect()
mentions = con.execute(f"SELECT * FROM '{TALLY}/mentions.parquet'").df()
files = con.execute(f"SELECT * FROM '{TALLY}/files.parquet'").df()
usage = pd.read_csv(TALLY / "usage_by_package.csv")
presence = pd.read_csv(TALLY / "language_presence.csv")
frame = pd.read_csv("../data/frame/frame.csv")

n_deposits = files["dataset_doi"].nunique()
n_files = len(files)
n_mentions = len(mentions)
at_risk = (
    files[files["in_analysis_set"]]
    .groupby("language")["dataset_doi"]
    .nunique()
    .to_dict()
)

# A "mention" is not the same object across languages, so no total over all of
# them means anything. In R and Python a mention is an import statement; in
# Stata it is every command occurrence, because that is what a Stata program
# is, so a combined count would be a count of Stata's syntax.
#
# The comparable unit is a mention that *could* name a third-party package.
# That excludes Stata builtins, R and Python standard libraries, and programs
# defined inside the deposit -- none of which were ever candidates for registry
# resolution, so leaving them in the denominator deflates the unresolved rate
# by an order of magnitude -- both figures are computed below.
NOT_THIRD_PARTY = ("builtin", "base_or_stdlib", "local_program")
candidates = mentions[~mentions["resolution"].isin(NOT_THIRD_PARTY)]
mentions_by_language = mentions.groupby("language").size().to_dict()

# Computed, not typed. The naive rate is quoted in the text to show how much
# the denominator matters, so it has to move when the data does -- a stale
# literal there would be the same error the passage is about.
naive_unknown_share = mentions["resolution"].eq("unknown").mean()
stata_mentions_per_file = mentions_by_language.get("stata", 0) / max(
    1, files[files["language"] == "stata"]["file_uid"].nunique()
)
r_mentions_per_file = mentions_by_language.get("r", 0) / max(
    1, files[files["language"] == "r"]["file_uid"].nunique()
)
# The released index's own size, read from the index rather than typed, so the
# paper cannot disagree with the artifact it cites.
INDEX = "../registries/snapshots/ssc/stata_command_index.parquet"
n_ssc_packages, n_ssc_commands = con.execute(
    f"SELECT count(DISTINCT package), count(DISTINCT command) "
    f"FROM '{INDEX}' WHERE NOT is_helper"
).fetchone()
# Quoted in Validation, so computed rather than typed.
n_stata_builtin_calls = int(
    (mentions["language"].eq("stata") & mentions["resolution"].eq("builtin")).sum()
)
# How much of the builtin list came from asking StataCorp rather than from
# curation. Read from the snapshot so it cannot drift from the artifact.
_verified = json.loads(
    Path("../registries/snapshots/stata_official/official.json").read_text()
)
# Against the *curated* list, not the shipped builtins.json -- that file is
# the merged set and already contains these names, so comparing to it returns
# zero and silently understates the whole point. This equals the official
# count because the crawl only asked about names that were unresolved or
# SSC-attributed; anything the curated list already knew was never queried.
n_verified_added = len(
    {n for n, ok in _verified["commands"].items() if ok} - set(curated().forms)
)
# The counterfactual quoted in Validation: what the unresolved rate would be
# with the curated list alone. It cannot be read off the tally -- it needs
# re-resolving -- so it is reconstructed rather than typed, which is the only
# way a comparison like this stays true after the next rebuild.
#
# Commands that are builtin only because the help server confirmed them rejoin
# the candidate pool. Those the SSC index also claims would have been credited
# to a package (the precision error); the rest would have read as unresolved.
_ssc_commands = {
    r[0]
    for r in con.execute(
        f"SELECT DISTINCT lower(command) FROM '{INDEX}' WHERE NOT is_helper"
    ).fetchall()
}
_readded = mentions[
    mentions["language"].eq("stata")
    & mentions["resolution"].eq("builtin")
    & ~mentions["normalized_name"].isin(set(curated().forms))
]
n_misattributed = int(_readded["normalized_name"].isin(_ssc_commands).sum())
curated_only_share = (
    candidates["resolution"].eq("unknown").sum() + len(_readded) - n_misattributed
) / (len(candidates) + len(_readded))

# Evidence for the archive-cap limitation: do bigger archives just hold more
# data, or more code too? Joined from the ledger, because the archives
# themselves are deleted after extraction.
#
# This was carried as a typed literal ("21 files to 221") measured on an
# earlier, smaller corpus. Recomputed here it is 13 to 41 -- the direction
# survives, the magnitude did not, which is the argument for computing it.
_ledger = {}
for _line in Path("../corpus/zenodo/ledger.jsonl").read_text().splitlines():
    if _line.strip():
        _r = json.loads(_line)
        _ledger["zenodo:" + _r["dataset_doi"].rsplit(".", 1)[-1]] = _r
_per_deposit = files.groupby("dataset_doi").size()
_sized = sorted(
    (_ledger[d]["bytes_fetched"], n)
    for d, n in _per_deposit.items()
    if d in _ledger and (_ledger[d].get("bytes_fetched") or 0) > 0
)
_q = max(1, len(_sized) // 4)
code_files_smallest = int(pd.Series([n for _, n in _sized[:_q]]).median())
code_files_largest = int(pd.Series([n for _, n in _sized[3 * _q :]]).median())

# Deposit-level coverage, by reason. A deposit that yielded nothing is not a
# finding about the deposit until you can say why, and the reasons are not
# interchangeable: an over-cap archive is a policy choice we made, a spanned
# archive is a format we declined to reassemble, and a failure is a bug or an
# outage. Reported as a table rather than one "coverage" number, because
# collapsing them lets a bug hide inside a stated limitation.
#
# Read from the ledger alone. The first version of this asked which deposits
# were absent from `files.parquet` and labelled the remainder "no code files
# in the deposit" -- which quietly counted 99 deposits collected after the
# tally was last built, plus 136 records that are not outcomes at all but
# requeue markers left by an earlier cap raise, carrying no counts and only
# surviving because the ledger takes the last write for a DOI. Comparing two
# artifacts built at different times measures the interval between them; the
# ledger is internally consistent, so it is the one to ask.
_last = {}
for _line in Path("../corpus/zenodo/ledger.jsonl").read_text().splitlines():
    if _line.strip():
        _r = json.loads(_line)
        _last[_r["dataset_doi"]] = _r
_reason_of = (
    ("n_skipped_over_cap", "archive over the size cap"),
    ("n_spanned", "multi-part archive, not reassembled"),
    ("n_failed", "download or extraction failed"),
)
_gaps = []
for _r in _last.values():
    if "n_candidate" not in _r:
        _gaps.append("awaiting re-collection")
        continue
    if _r["n_fetched"]:
        continue
    _why = next(
        (label for key, label in _reason_of if _r.get(key)),
        "deposit contains no code files",
    )
    _gaps.append(_why)
coverage = (
    pd.Series(_gaps).value_counts().rename_axis("reason").reset_index(name="deposits")
)
n_deposits_declared = len(_last)
n_deposits_collected = len(_last) - len(_gaps)
share_collected = n_deposits_collected / len(_last)
n_spanned_deposits = sum(1 for _r in _last.values() if _r.get("n_spanned"))

# The findings paragraphs. Every claim there is a computation here, including
# the qualitative one: which of the top Stata packages are output formatters
# is a fixed, checkable list of names, not a judgement made at writing time.
_at_risk = dict(zip(presence["language"], presence["n_deposits"], strict=True))
n_stata_deposits = int(_at_risk.get("stata", 0))
n_r_deposits = int(_at_risk.get("r", 0))
n_python_deposits = int(_at_risk.get("python", 0))
stata_to_r_ratio = n_stata_deposits / max(1, n_r_deposits)


def _top(language: str, n: int = 10):
    return usage[usage["language"] == language].nlargest(n, "n_deposits")


_top_stata = _top("stata")
n_top_stata = len(_top_stata)
top_stata_package = f"`{_top_stata.iloc[0]['package']}`"
top_stata_share = float(_top_stata.iloc[0]["share_of_deposits"])
_top_python = _top("python")
top_python_package = f"`{_top_python.iloc[0]['package']}`"
top_python_share = float(_top_python.iloc[0]["share_of_deposits"])

#: Stata packages whose purpose is formatting results for publication rather
#: than estimating anything. Named explicitly so the claim is falsifiable: a
#: reader can disagree with the membership of this set and recompute.
TABLE_MAKERS = {
    "estout",
    "outreg2",
    "coefplot",
    "tabout",
    "asdoc",
    "outtable",
    "esttab",
    "mktab",
    "xml_tab",
    "logout",
    "putexcel",
    "outreg",
}
_found_makers = [p for p in _top_stata["package"] if p in TABLE_MAKERS]
n_table_makers = len(_found_makers)
table_makers_list = ", ".join(f"`{p}`" for p in _found_makers)

# The unresolved rate per *deposit*, which is the unit this paper argues for
# everywhere else and then quietly abandoned here. Pooling over mentions lets
# one deposit speak for the corpus, and one did until vendored library trees
# stopped being read as research code -- a deposit shipping a copy of Stata's
# `ado/base` contributed 46% of all unresolved Stata mentions by itself.
_per_deposit = (
    candidates.assign(unresolved=candidates["resolution"].eq("unknown"))
    .groupby("dataset_doi")["unresolved"]
    .agg(["size", "sum"])
)
_per_deposit["rate"] = _per_deposit["sum"] / _per_deposit["size"]
median_deposit_unresolved = float(_per_deposit["rate"].median())
p90_deposit_unresolved = float(_per_deposit["rate"].quantile(0.9))
share_deposits_fully_resolved = float((_per_deposit["sum"] == 0).mean())

# Named in Validation. The most *widespread* unresolved Stata name, ranked by
# deposits rather than mentions: one deposit calling something six hundred
# times is one user of it, and a mention-ranked list is a ranking of whichever
# deposits are largest.
_stata_unknown = mentions[
    (mentions["language"] == "stata") & (mentions["resolution"] == "unknown")
]
_by_deposits = _stata_unknown.groupby("normalized_name")["dataset_doi"].nunique()
top_unresolved_stata = f"`{_by_deposits.idxmax()}`"
n_grc1leg_deposits = int(_by_deposits.max())
stata_unknown_share_of_all = len(_stata_unknown) / max(
    1, int(candidates["resolution"].eq("unknown").sum())
)

# The two categories that exist so that "we cannot name a package" is not
# confused with "there is no package here". Both were folded into `unknown`
# until the construct was allowed to reach the resolver.
n_local_relative = int(mentions["resolution"].eq("local_relative").sum())
n_dynamic = int(mentions["resolution"].eq("dynamic").sum())

# R's own parser as a true oracle for the syntactic task. Unlike the `renv`
# comparison below this is not a peer agreement: R's parser defines the
# answer, so disagreement is our error and the rate is exact.
_oracle = json.loads(Path("../build/validation/r_oracle.json").read_text())
n_oracle_files = _oracle["n_files_compared"]
n_oracle_unparseable = _oracle["n_files_unparseable_by_r"]
n_oracle_pairs = _oracle["true_positives"] + _oracle["false_negatives"]
oracle_precision = _oracle["precision"]
oracle_recall = _oracle["recall"]

# Cross-tool agreement, read from the artifact `scripts_validate_renv.py`
# writes. This paragraph used to carry a typed 0.998 that nothing in the
# repository computed -- no script, no artifact, no recorded run. It was the
# one number here with no provenance at all, and it was wrong by about a
# tenth; the check that caught it is `tests/test_paper.py`, which fails on any
# bare numeral left in the prose.
_renv = json.loads(Path("../build/validation/renv_agreement.json").read_text())
n_renv_compared = _renv["n_deposits_compared"]
renv_mean_jaccard = _renv["mean_jaccard"]
renv_pooled_jaccard = _renv["pooled_jaccard"]
renv_perfect_share = _renv["n_perfect_agreement"] / _renv["n_deposits_compared"]
renv_version = _renv["renv_version"]

# Named in Limitations: Stata keywords reaching command position. Computed,
# so that closing one of the gaps shows up here rather than leaving a stale
# boast in the prose.
_keyword_noise = _stata_unknown[_stata_unknown["normalized_name"].isin(
    {"in", "using", "str"}
)]
n_keyword_noise = len(_keyword_noise)
n_keyword_noise_deposits = int(_keyword_noise["dataset_doi"].nunique())

# Named in Limitations. Computed so the claim cannot go stale silently.
# Written as a computed sentence rather than two typed package names, so a
# false positive that gets fixed disappears from the prose instead of being
# reported as affecting zero deposits. `wordy` did exactly that once vendored
# library code stopped being read as research code.
_KNOWN_FALSE_POSITIVES = {"fastcd": "c", "wordy": "word"}
_residual = {
    pkg: int(
        mentions[
            (mentions["language"] == "stata") & (mentions["resolved_package"] == pkg)
        ]["dataset_doi"].nunique()
    )
    for pkg in _KNOWN_FALSE_POSITIVES
}
residual_false_positives = (
    ", ".join(
        f"`{pkg}` (command `{_KNOWN_FALSE_POSITIVES[pkg]}`) in {n} deposits"
        for pkg, n in sorted(_residual.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])
        if n
    )
    or "none"
)
stata_builtin_share = (
    mentions[mentions["language"] == "stata"]["resolution"].eq("builtin").mean()
)
```

## The credit problem

The most widely used piece of third-party software in social science
replication code is a table formatter. `{python} top_stata_package` appears in
`{python} f"{top_stata_share:.0%}"` of the Stata deposits we collected, ahead
of every estimator. Whatever we currently reward, it is not what we think.

We could not have told you that a year ago, because nobody could count it.
That is the problem this paper is about.

Research runs on software that its authors are not credited for
[@howison2011; @smith2016], and credit is what gets software written. Someone
choosing between a paper and a package is choosing between something their
department knows how to value and something it does not. Better counts of use
would change that calculation, which makes the counts worth getting right
[@sood_countpy].

The counts available today are weak in a specific way. Downloads measure
fetches, not use, and reward frequent releases; a package can double its
numbers by cutting more versions. Prose mentions in articles [@schindler2022]
capture what an author remembered to name in a methods section. Neither
establishes that the software ran.

Replication code does. A deposit attached to a published paper at a journal
whose data-and-code policy an editor actually verifies is the strongest
routine evidence that a package was used in research
[@stodden2018; @vilhuber2020]. We call this **validated use**, and this paper
is about measuring it across R, Python and Stata.

## What validated use means

The estimand:

> Among replication deposits in collection *J* containing at least one
> analyzable script in language *L*, the share that statically reference
> package *P*.

The unit is the deposit, not the mention. A deposit calling `ggplot2` two
hundred times is one user of `ggplot2`, and a mention-weighted count would
rank whichever deposits happen to be largest.

Static reference is not execution. A deposit may load a package in a
superseded script, inside a dead branch, or in setup code that never runs, and
code kept out of the deposit is invisible to us. A replication package is a
curated artifact rather than a forensic copy of an environment
[@trisovic2022]. Reachability from master scripts is reported as a sensitivity
analysis, which bounds dead code without pretending to observe execution.

Reference also means direct reference. A deposit loading `fixest` also runs
`Rcpp` and `sandwich`, and neither is counted. That is the right choice for a
credit metric: what an author chose and what their choice pulled in are
different quantities, and crediting the closure would hand the top of the
table to whatever the popular packages happen to depend on.

Expanding the closure is a separate exercise, and possible in two of our three
languages. R declares dependencies in `DESCRIPTION`, Python in a
distribution's `requires_dist`, and both can be walked mechanically. An SSC
`.pkg` manifest records them, when it records them at all, as prose in a
free-text field. The `reghdfe` manifest reads
`Requires: Stata version 11.2 and ftools from SSC (q.v.)`, so extracting a
graph from it means parsing English.

The closest prior work executed R code from over 2,000 Harvard Dataverse
deposits to study reproducibility [@trisovic2022]. We take a similar corpus
and ask which libraries the code references, across three languages rather
than one.

## What we found

```{python}
#| label: top-packages
rows = []
for lang in ("stata", "r", "python"):
    top = usage[usage["language"] == lang].nlargest(10, "n_deposits")
    for _, r in top.iterrows():
        rows.append({
            "language": lang,
            "package": r["package"],
            "deposits": int(r["n_deposits"]),
            "of": int(r["n_deposits_at_risk"]),
            "share": f"{r['share_of_deposits']:.0%}",
        })
_top = pd.DataFrame(rows)
_top.columns = ["language", "package", "deposits", "of", "share"]
table(
    _top,
    caption="Most used third-party packages, by language",
    label="tab:top-packages",
    note=(
        "The ten packages appearing in the most deposits in each language. "
        "\\emph{deposits} counts deposits referencing the package; "
        "\\emph{of} is the number of deposits containing analyzable code in "
        "that language, which is the only denominator these shares are "
        "comparable against. A deposit counts once however many times it "
        "calls the package."
    ),
)
```

Every count is a share of the deposits **at risk**, meaning those that contain
analyzable code in that language. A share against any other denominator is not
comparable to anything.

### The most-used research software formats tables

```{python}
#| label: fig-credit
figure(
    "figures/credit.pdf",
    caption="The twelve most used Stata packages, by share of deposits",
    label="fig:credit",
    note=(
        "Packages whose purpose is presenting results rather than estimating "
        "anything are filled dark. Counts to the right of each bar are "

    ),

```

Of the ten most widely used Stata packages (\cref{tab:top-packages}), `{python} f"{n_table_makers}"`
exist to format output rather than to estimate anything:
`{python} table_makers_list`. The ordering is the finding, and \cref{fig:credit} is the ordering. The
single most used is `{python} top_stata_package`, in `{python} f"{top_stata_share:.0%}"` of Stata
deposits, ahead of every regression command.

This is worth sitting with if the point of counting is credit. A large part of
what research depends on is the machinery for turning estimates into a
publishable exhibit, and that machinery is written by people whose CVs say
they wrote a package nobody cites.

### Stata is the majority language and the one nobody counts

```{python}
#| label: fig-languages
figure(
    "figures/languages.pdf",
    caption="Languages by repository, and so by discipline",
    label="fig:languages",
    note=(
        "Share of deposits containing at least one analyzable file in each "
        "language. Zenodo's verified collections are economics journals; the "
        "Harvard Dataverse collections are mostly political science. A "
        "deposit may contain more than one language, so the bars within a "
        "repository do not sum to one hundred."
    ),
)
```

`{python} f"{n_stata_deposits:,}"` deposits contain analyzable Stata against
`{python} f"{n_r_deposits:,}"` with R and
`{python} f"{n_python_deposits:,}"` with Python, roughly
`{python} f"{stata_to_r_ratio:.1f}"` Stata deposits for every R one, and
\cref{fig:languages} shows the split is disciplinary rather than incidental.

Studies of research software cover R and Python, the two languages with public
registries. That omission is not a random sample of the field. It removes the
language most of this literature is written in, and it removes it precisely
because counting it is harder, which is a bad reason for a discipline to be
invisible.

### Concentration differs by language, for reasons about denominators

`{python} top_python_package` appears in
`{python} f"{top_python_share:.0%}"` of Python deposits, because Python in a
replication package almost always means a dataframe pipeline. Stata's most
common package reaches `{python} f"{top_stata_share:.0%}"` with a much longer
tail, because Stata does natively what a Python deposit must import a library
to do.

Reading those two numbers as "Python users are more consistent" would be a
mistake. They are shares of different kinds of deposit, and the languages are
not substitutes for one another here.

### Some of the most-used software is in no registry at all

`{python} top_unresolved_stata` is the most widespread Stata command we cannot
resolve to any package, and it appears in
`{python} f"{n_grc1leg_deposits}"` deposits. It is not obscure. It is
distributed from StataCorp's own website and indexed nowhere. Below it the
pattern holds: `dcdensity` from its author's page, `btscs` from a replication
archive, `prvalue` and `listcoef` from a suite that ships with a textbook.

A credit system built on registries cannot see any of them, and no amount of
indexing SSC more carefully will help, because they were never on SSC. This
is the ceiling on what anyone can currently count about Stata, and it is a
fact about the ecosystem rather than a gap in our method. R and Python have
nothing comparable: a package outside CRAN or PyPI is unusual enough to be
remarkable.

## What better counts are for

Two uses, and the first is the one the counts were built for.

Software authors can be credited against something defensible. A package in
`{python} f"{top_stata_share:.0%}"` of the Stata deposits at policy-verified
journals is a stronger claim on a CV than a download count, and it is a claim
a committee can check. The tables here are released so that any package's
number can be looked up rather than asserted.

The second use is targeting. Work on software reliability has to choose what
to examine, and choosing by reputation reproduces whatever the field already
believes. Our sibling project `kasauti` runs a battery of probes against every
release of a package to find where results silently changed, and it picks its
targets partly by how often a function appears in real code. Validated-use
counts answer that question on purpose instead of by hand, and they point at
the packages where a quiet change would touch the most published work.

## Sampling frame

```{python}
#| label: frame-table
located = frame[frame["collection_id"].notna() & (frame["collection_id"] != "")]
zen = located[located["source"] == "zenodo"]
unlocated = frame[frame["notes"].fillna("").str.startswith("unlocated")]

# The Dataverse half of the frame, enumerated collection by collection rather
# than declared: one request returns a journal's whole dataset list, so these
# are counted deposits and not an estimate.
_dv_path = Path("../data/frame/dataverse_deposits.csv")
dv = pd.read_csv(_dv_path) if _dv_path.exists() else pd.DataFrame()
n_dv_deposits = len(dv)
n_dv_collections = dv["collection_id"].nunique() if len(dv) else 0
n_frame_total = int(zen["n_records_declared"].sum()) + n_dv_deposits
```

The inclusion rule is not ours. We take the journal list maintained by the
**Social Science Data Editors** in the Data and Code Availability Standard:
journals whose data-and-code policy the editors *actively verify*. That is a
criterion a reader can check, and it avoids the trap of a frame assembled from
whatever a keyword search happened to return.

The frame spans two repositories, which is not a convenience: they hold
different disciplines. Zenodo's verified collections are economics;
Harvard Dataverse's journal collections are mostly political science, and a
study of only one would describe a field while claiming to describe social
science.

| repository | collections | deposits |
|---|---:|---:|
| Zenodo | `{python} len(zen)` | `{python} f"{int(zen['n_records_declared'].sum()):,}"` |
| Harvard Dataverse | `{python} f"{n_dv_collections}"` | `{python} f"{n_dv_deposits:,}"` |
| **total** | | **`{python} f"{n_frame_total:,}"`** |

The Dataverse figure is enumerated rather than declared. One request returns
a journal collection's entire dataset list, so these are deposits we counted,
not an estimate we were given, and where a collection was too large for that
single listing, it was paged instead.

Two things the enumeration found are worth recording, because a frame that
only reports its successes is not a frame. One journal collection present in
a 2024 snapshot, `regionalstatistics`, no longer exists: Harvard answers
"Can't find dataverse with identifier". And six collections returned nothing
on one pass, of which five succeeded minutes later, transient, and
distinguished from the one that is genuinely gone, because retrying the first
kind works and retrying the second never will.

`{python} len(unlocated)` DCAS journals are recorded as **unlocated** rather
than omitted: eight AEA titles live on openICPSR, and two we could not place.
A coverage gap belongs in the frame as a row, not in a silence.

Every collection is verified before use. Zenodo does not reject an unknown
`communities=` filter, it ignores it and returns all 7.1 million records, so
an unverified slug would substitute the entire archive for one journal, an error
shaped like abundance.


Of `{python} f"{n_deposits_declared:,}"` Zenodo deposits attempted,
`{python} f"{n_deposits_collected:,}"`
(`{python} f"{share_collected:.0%}"`) yielded files. \Cref{tab:coverage} itemises the rest
rather than summarising them, because the reasons are not interchangeable. A size
cap is a choice we made, an unreassembled multi-part archive is a format we
declined to handle, and a failure is a bug or an outage.

```{python}
#| label: coverage
table(
    coverage,
    caption="Why a deposit yielded no code",
    label="tab:coverage",
    note=(
        "Zenodo deposits that produced no analyzable file, by reason. The "
        "size cap and the unreassembled multi-part archives are choices we "
        "made and are recoverable; the single failure is a zip using a "
        "compression method Python does not implement."
    ),
)
```

## Measurement

| language | mechanism |
|---|---|
| R | `tree-sitter` syntax walk |
| Python | stdlib `ast`, `tokenize` fallback |
| Stata | purpose-built lexer + SSC command→package index |
| `.Rmd`/`.qmd`/`.Rnw` | knitr chunk splitter, routed per engine |
| `.ipynb` | per-cell, kernel language from metadata |

Two choices carry most of the weight.

**Strings and comments are excluded structurally, not by pre-stripping.** In a
syntax tree, `cat("run library(dplyr)")` is a call whose argument is a string
node; those bytes never form a call, so a walk over call nodes cannot see them.
Regex-based detection has no such guarantee, and the difference is measurable
(see the validation section).

**Stata required building an artifact that did not exist.** R has CRAN and
Python has PyPI, but Stata has no machine-readable registry. We reconstruct a
command→package index from SSC distribution manifests, `{python} f"{n_ssc_packages:,}"` packages and
`{python} f"{n_ssc_commands:,}"` commands, and release it. Without it, Stata is
unmeasurable, which is why prior work has omitted the language social science
uses most.

## Validation {#sec-baseline}

```{python}
#| label: resolution
res = candidates["resolution"].value_counts()
resolved = res.get("known_current", 0) + res.get("known_archived", 0)
unknown_share = res.get("unknown", 0) / len(candidates)
by_language = (
    candidates.assign(unresolved=candidates["resolution"].eq("unknown"))
    .groupby("language")["unresolved"]
    .agg(["size", "sum"])
)
by_language["rate"] = (by_language["sum"] / by_language["size"]).map("{:.1%}".format)
by_language.columns = ["candidate mentions", "unresolved", "rate"]
_res = by_language.sort_values("candidate mentions", ascending=False).reset_index()
_res.columns = ["language", "candidate mentions", "unresolved", "rate"]
table(
    _res,
    caption="Mentions that could name a package, and those we could not resolve",
    label="tab:resolution",
    note=(
        "Restricted to mentions that could name a third-party package, so "
        "Stata builtins, standard libraries and programs a deposit defines "
        "itself are excluded from both columns. An unresolved mention is one "
        "we cannot attribute, not evidence that no package exists."
    ),
)
```

We report what these checks can establish and no more.

**Registry resolution** is coverage, not precision: a local module can share a
name with a real distribution. `{python} f"{unknown_share:.1%}"` of
third-party-candidate mentions resolve to no registry, and every such name is
enumerated rather than dropped.

The denominator matters more than the rate. Against *all* mentions the same
figure is `{python} f"{naive_unknown_share:.1%}"`, which would be a flattering
way to describe the identical data: it divides by
`{python} f"{n_stata_builtin_calls:,}"` Stata builtin calls that were never
candidates for registry resolution and could not have been unresolved. We
report the rate against mentions that could name a package, which is
`{python} f"{unknown_share / naive_unknown_share:.0f}"` times larger and is the
number a reader should use to discount our coverage.

**So does the unit.** Per deposit -- the unit this paper uses everywhere
else, for the reason it gives for package rankings -- the distribution is not
centred anywhere near the pooled figure:

| statistic | unresolved share |
|---|---:|
| pooled over mentions | `{python} f"{unknown_share:.1%}"` |
| median deposit | `{python} f"{median_deposit_unresolved:.1%}"` |
| 90th-percentile deposit | `{python} f"{p90_deposit_unresolved:.1%}"` |
| deposits fully resolved | `{python} f"{share_deposits_fully_resolved:.0%}"` |

`{python} f"{share_deposits_fully_resolved:.0%}"` of deposits have **every**
candidate mention resolved. The pooled figure is not wrong, but it describes a
minority of deposits and should be read as an upper bound on how much of a
typical deposit we cannot name, not as a typical value.

The rate differs by language in a way a pooled figure hides, and the reasons
differ with it.

**Stata carries almost all of it**, `{python} f"{stata_unknown_share_of_all:.0%}"` of unresolved mentions, and
what remains there is mostly not our error. It is a property of the Stata
ecosystem, and it is the second half of the argument the command→package
index makes.

The most widespread unresolved command is
`{python} top_unresolved_stata`, in `{python} f"{n_grc1leg_deposits}"`
deposits: a real, widely used program distributed from StataCorp's own
website and indexed in no machine-readable registry, SSC included. Below it
the pattern holds, `dcdensity` from its author's page, `btscs` from a
replication archive, `prvalue` and `listcoef` from the SPost suite
distributed with a textbook. These are not obscure. They are ordinary tools
in political science and economics, and no amount of indexing SSC will find
them, because they were never on SSC.

That is worth stating plainly rather than reporting as coverage. R has CRAN,
Python has PyPI, and a package outside those registries is unusual enough to
be remarkable. Stata's third-party ecosystem has a substantial tail that
lives on personal pages, textbook companion sites and the vendor's own
server, and any measurement of Stata software use, ours or anyone's, is
bounded by that rather than by how carefully the indexing is done. The
remainder of the unresolved names are lexer error, enumerated in the
limitations below rather than netted out.

**Names that no package could ever have.** A mention is unresolved when we
cannot name a package for it, which is not the same as there being one. Two
constructs make that distinction explicit rather than letting it inflate the
rate: `{python} f"{n_local_relative:,}"` Python relative imports
(`from .models import Constants` names a module in the deposit, not a
distribution) and `{python} f"{n_dynamic:,}"` names built at run time
(`library(pkg, character.only = TRUE)`, where the package is a variable and
no static analysis can know it). Both are reported in their own categories.
Folding them into `unknown`, which an earlier version of this pipeline did, overstates the unresolved rate and, worse, credits some of them to real
packages that happen to share the name: `models`, `results` and `log` are all
distributions on PyPI as well as things people call their own files.

**The official-command list is measured, not curated.** Stata's builtin list
is the one place where an omission is not neutral: a command that official
Stata provides but our list lacks falls through to the SSC index, and if some
package happens to ship a file of that name, it is attributed there. Rather
than curate from memory we checked every command in the corpus against
StataCorp's public help server, which is authoritative in the only way that
matters, it is the vendor's own answer.

This mattered more than expected. It moved
`{python} f"{n_verified_added}"` commands out of "resolves to nothing",
including `ds`, `pca` and `testparm`, and it removed every case where a
command claimed by both official Stata and an SSC package had been credited to
the package. With the curated list alone the unresolved rate on this same
corpus is `{python} f"{curated_only_share:.1%}"` rather than
`{python} f"{unknown_share:.1%}"`, and
`{python} f"{n_misattributed:,}"` mentions would have been credited to an SSC
package that merely ships a file of the same name. Much of what looked like a
coverage gap was our own ignorance of Stata, not a limit of the method.

The check is not a status code. Every query returns HTTP 200, including for
names that do not exist, so existence is read from the body text; and the
server documents concepts and functions as well as commands, so pages from the
User's Guide and function manuals are excluded. Without that second filter the
system variables `_n` and `_b` and the function `e()` are reported as official
Stata commands.

**Cross-tool agreement** with `renv::dependencies()`
(`{python} renv_version`) over
`{python} f"{n_renv_compared:,}"` corpus R deposits gives a mean per-deposit
Jaccard of `{python} f"{renv_mean_jaccard:.2f}"` and a pooled Jaccard of
`{python} f"{renv_pooled_jaccard:.2f}"`;
`{python} f"{renv_perfect_share:.0%}"` of deposits agree exactly. Both are
reported because they answer different questions: the mean weights every
deposit equally, the pooled figure every package-deposit pair, so a headline
cannot be flattered by deposits with one obvious package in them.

This is *convergent validity, not accuracy*. `renv` performs the same kind of
static scan over the same files and shares the same blind spots, a package
named only in a string, or loaded through a variable, is invisible to both, so agreement measures whether two implementations of one idea agree, not
whether either is right. What it can catch is an implementation error on our
side large enough to show against an independent codebase, which is why the
per-deposit disagreements are written out rather than reduced to the
headline.

**Syntactic accuracy has a true oracle, and we use it.** For "does this file
contain a call to `library` whose argument is `x`", R's own parser is not a
peer but the definition of the answer, so disagreement is our error and the
error rate is exact rather than indicative. Running R's parser over
`{python} f"{n_oracle_files:,}"` corpus `.R` files and recursing its
expression trees gives precision `{python} f"{oracle_precision:.4f}"` and
recall `{python} f"{oracle_recall:.4f}"` across
`{python} f"{n_oracle_pairs:,}"` name-file pairs.

A further `{python} f"{n_oracle_unparseable:,}"` files R itself could not
parse. Those are excluded rather than scored: an unparseable file is not a
file with no dependencies, and counting it as one would credit us for finding
nothing in it.

**How that figure was reached matters as much as its value.** Perfect
agreement is what a comparison looks like when the comparison is broken, so
the working is worth stating. Five disagreements were adjudicated by consulting
R's behaviour directly, and four of the five were the oracle's fault: it
unboxed a one-element result into a bare string, so a lone `LearnBayes` was
read as eight packages named after its letters; it skipped every
`character.only = TRUE` call, though a string literal there is still a literal;
it could not see through `base::library(c)`, because such a call's head is
itself a call; and it never descended into a function's formals, hiding every
`pkg::fun()` used as a default argument. One was ours: `"m"::baz()` is legal R
and we dropped it. Where the two disagreed about `requireNamespace(pkg)` we
ran R rather than reasoning: `library(pkg)` with `pkg <- "stats"` errors, so
the symbol is the name, while `requireNamespace(pkg)` returns `TRUE`, so the
symbol is a variable.

A number tuned against the same data it scores is worth little, so the
extractor is also checked against ground truth we did not write: `renv`'s own
test fixture, which enumerates thirteen loader spellings and states in its
comments which must be found. That check failed where the oracle had not,
because a blind spot two implementations share is indistinguishable from
agreement, it found `xfun::pkg_attach(c("g", "h"))` and `pkg_attach2("i",
"j")` unhandled. Both now are, and the fixture is a test.

This bounds one thing exactly, whether our tree-sitter walk sees what R sees, and nothing else. It says nothing about Stata, nothing about resolution
against CRAN, and nothing about whether a `library()` call means the analysis
used the package.

**What we do not claim.** We have not hand-labelled a probability sample, so we
report no human-validated precision or recall against research *use*. That is a
deliberate deferral; the labelling frame is designed and can be run.

## Limitations

Static reference is not execution. The reachability analysis bounds that gap
rather than closing it.

Deposits whose only content exceeds the archive size cap yield no code, and
the tail this excludes is not data without code. Code files scale with archive
size: a median of `{python} f"{code_files_smallest}"` code files in the
smallest quartile of archives against `{python} f"{code_files_largest}"` in
the largest. The gap therefore runs against large, code-heavy projects rather
than against large datasets.

Multi-part archives are not reassembled.
`{python} f"{n_spanned_deposits}"` deposits split a package across `.z01`,
`.7z.002` or `.partN.rar` segments. Only the tail segment carries the central
directory, so it downloads at exactly the size the repository states, lists
every member, and fails on the first read. That looks like a corrupt download
and is not one. We count these rather than retrying them, since no number of
retries can assemble one segment.

Stata resolution reflects today's status, not the status when the code was
written. A command that was user-written in 2010 and later absorbed into
official Stata resolves against what it is now, which can manufacture a trend
for anyone reading these counts over time.

Two false positives survive, and we name them rather than suppress them.
SSC packages whose only command is a single common token attract stray matches
from Mata-style bare assignments outside a `mata:` block, which the lexer
cannot recognise as Mata. Currently `{python} residual_false_positives`.
A rule against single-letter commands would hide the next instance instead of
surfacing it, and because the count is computed, the list shrinks on its own
as causes are fixed.

Three lexer gaps remain open and countable. Stata keywords reach command
position in contexts the lexer does not model: `in` and `using` after an
old-style `/* */` line continuation, and `str` inside an `infile dictionary`
block, where a line such as `str FACT_ID 5-12` declares a storage type rather
than calling anything. Together that is `{python} f"{n_keyword_noise:,}"`
mentions across `{python} f"{n_keyword_noise_deposits}"` deposits. They
inflate the unresolved rate and nothing else, because a keyword cannot
collide with an SSC package name and so none is misattributed. Reporting the
number is worth more than a blocklist that would suppress the symptom and
leave the contexts unmodelled.

MATLAB, SAS and SPSS are reported as language presence only. MATLAB has no
import statement and no resolvable registry, so attributing toolboxes would be
unbounded error.

## Data and code availability

The Stata command-to-package index is deposited at
[10.5281/zenodo.21926100](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21926100) under CC0,
with `{python} f"{n_ssc_commands:,}"` commands across
`{python} f"{n_ssc_packages:,}"` packages. It is released separately from
this paper because its usefulness does not depend on this corpus: anyone
counting Stata needs the same mapping.

The extraction pipeline, the resolver, the frame and the per-package counts
are at <https://github.com/recite/softverse>. Package-level counts can be
looked up directly rather than read off a table, which is the point of
producing them: a credit metric nobody can query is an assertion.

## Reproducibility

The corpus, the registry snapshots and the extractor version are pinned. Every
mention carries the extractor version, grammar version and registry lock that
produced it, plus its source line and a snippet, so any number here can be
traced to the text it came from without re-running anything.

```{python}
#| label: provenance
lock = json.loads(Path("../registries/registries.lock.json").read_text())
table(
    pd.DataFrame([{"registry": k, "sha256": v[:16]} for k, v in lock.items()]),
    caption="Pinned registry snapshots",
    label="tab:provenance",
    note=(
        "Every mention carries the lock identifier of the registry snapshot "
        "it was resolved against, so a count can be reproduced against the "
        "registry as it stood rather than as it stands."
    ),
    align="ll",
)
```
